failure_summary.description: Missed the force of universal scope and added an unsupported converse claiming every listed divisor occurs.
Either rejected a stronger true claim for a weaker one or accepted extra detail without establishing it.
Did not correctly apply the stated hypothesis when identifying the equivalent complexity bound.
Relied on misremembered quantitative bounds rather than verifying the exact estimate and its direction.

patch.reasoning: The recurring issue is choosing an option based on plausibility or apparent strength instead of verifying every clause under the exact hypotheses and quantifiers. The edits add a truth-before-strength check, explicit quantifier auditing, and safeguards for theorem-dependent quantitative claims.

edits.content:
## Verify Every Clause and Quantifier
Translate each option into its individual claims and record the scope of each quantifier and parameter range. Treat words such as “every,” “some,” “only,” and “conversely” as substantive: an added universal or converse claim must be proved independently. One false extra clause makes the whole option false.

## Choose the Strongest True Option
First determine which options are actually supported; only then compare their strength. Do not select an option merely because it is more detailed, nor retreat to a weaker claim based on a speculative obstruction. When options are nested, select the strongest one whose full statement is established, not the strongest one that sounds plausible.

## Check Hypotheses and Quantitative Bounds
Apply all stated hypotheses before invoking a characterization or theorem. For numerical estimates, verify the exact quantity, inequality direction, parameter range, and whether the bound is uniform or applies to the specific case. Do not invent citations or use a vaguely remembered bound to rule out an option.
